transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what's been troubling you that brought you here today?

Well… what’s been getting to me is my appearance, mostly my face and my hands. I know that might sound vain coming from a man my age, especially someone who’s worked outside most of his life, but I can’t seem to get past it. My skin just looks so rough and worn to me—cracks in my hands, spots, sagging in my face, all of it.

And when I have to go into town or deal with people at the bank or the county office, I get this feeling like they’re looking right at it. Like they’re noticing how beat-up I look, how old or weathered I seem. My wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, that it’s normal, but it doesn’t feel normal to me. It feels like it’s the first thing anybody sees.
When you look at your face or hands, do you see specific flaws or defects that you feel are very noticeable, even if others might not seem to notice them?

Yes… yes, I do. It’s not just a general “I’m getting older” kind of thing, though I suppose that’s part of it. It’s specific things. On my hands, I see the cracks, the rough patches, the spots, the way the skin looks thick and dried out, like old leather almost. And with my face, I notice the sagging and the weathered look around my cheeks and eyes, the spots there too. It all just looks so worn down to me.

And I know my wife says, “That’s just what happens when you’ve worked outside,” and maybe other people wouldn’t call it a defect exactly, but when I’m standing in front of someone at the bank or talking to somebody at a county office, I feel like that’s what they’re seeing first. Like they’re looking at my hands when I sign something, or at my face when I’m talking, and thinking I look rough or beat-up. I can’t seem to get past it.
Do these concerns about your appearance ever make it hard for you to do things like go out in public, interact with people, or do your job?

Yes… it has, more than I like to admit. It’s not just me feeling bad in the mirror and then going on with the day. There have been times I’ve missed calls with bankers, or let them go to voicemail, because I knew if I took the call it would lead to sitting down in person, signing papers, having them across the desk looking at my hands or my face. And then I’d tell myself I needed to clean up better first, or wait until my skin looked less cracked, or shave a certain way, or… I don’t know, just get myself looking acceptable enough to be seen.

And that spills over into the farm decisions too. I’ll put things off that need deciding because they involve meeting someone or going into an office. It sounds ridiculous saying it out loud, because these are practical things—banking, farm business, things that shouldn’t have anything to do with how I look—but in the moment it feels like I can’t make myself go sit in front of people like this.

I’ve also stopped agreeing to photos. We sometimes could use pictures for promoting the retreat and craft sales, and in the past I might have stood in for that, but now I’ll find reasons not to. I’ll say somebody else should be in it, or that I’m busy, or that the light isn’t right, but really it’s because I can’t stand the thought of my face or hands being in a photo people are going to look at. So yes, it’s gotten in the way. More than I wish it did.
Have you noticed that these concerns about your appearance have been making you feel down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy?

I’m not sure I’d say it’s hopeless, exactly. I mean… I don’t wake up thinking there’s no point to anything, if that’s what you mean. But it does wear on me. It kind of sits in the background, and then if I know I have to go somewhere or be seen, it comes right up to the front.

As far as feeling down, yes, I suppose I do feel pretty low about it sometimes. More embarrassed than anything, maybe. Frustrated with myself too, because part of me knows I’m 62 and I’ve worked with my hands my whole life, so of course my skin isn’t going to look like somebody who’s been indoors all day. But knowing that doesn’t seem to take the sting out of it.

Losing interest… I don’t know. I still care about the things I care about. It’s more that I might avoid parts of them if they mean being looked at or photographed or having to present myself. So I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped enjoying everything, but this concern definitely takes some of the ease out of things. It makes things feel heavier than they ought to.

When you’re worried about how your face or hands look, is it more that you feel certain specific parts of them are defective or unacceptably flawed, or is it more that you’re afraid people will judge you negatively just because of how you appear overall?

It’s both, I guess, but it starts with specific things. I’m not just thinking, “Oh, I don’t like how I look overall.” It’s the cracks in my hands, the spots, the roughness, the way they look worn out. And on my face it’s the sagging and the weathered look, the spots there too. Those are the things my eye goes right to, and then I can’t stop noticing them.

But once I’m around other people, it turns into this feeling that they’re judging the whole of me because of it. Like if I’m sitting across from a banker or someone at the county office, I’m thinking they’re noticing my hands when I sign something, or my face while I’m talking, and deciding I look rough or careless or just… old and beat-up. My wife tells me I look like a man who’s worked outdoors his whole life, and I know there’s truth in that. But it doesn’t feel that harmless to me when I’m the one being looked at. It feels like those flaws are right out front.

When you look at those specific parts of your face or hands, do you believe they look abnormal or defective in a way that most people would notice and judge, or do you feel like you're noticing flaws that others probably don’t even see?

I think… I think I believe they really do look abnormal, or at least bad enough that people would notice. That’s the part I keep getting stuck on. It doesn’t feel like I’m just picking out some tiny thing nobody else could possibly see. When I look at my hands, the cracks and spots and roughness are right there. They look worn down, like they don’t belong in a meeting room or across a desk from somebody in a clean shirt.

And my face too—the sagging, the weathered look, the spots. I know my wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors his whole life, and maybe that’s true in a practical sense. But when I’m sitting with a banker or someone from the county, I can’t make myself believe they aren’t seeing it. I picture them noticing every bit of it and judging me for it, like I look careless or rough or older than I should.

So… maybe other people don’t see it as harshly as I do. I can admit that’s possible. But in the moment, it feels very visible. It feels like it’s the first thing anyone would notice.
Can you tell me if there have been times when you’ve looked in the mirror and focused on these flaws, even when no one else has pointed them out or seemed to notice them?

Yes. That happens more than I like to admit. It’s not even always because somebody has said anything. Most of the time nobody has said a word. I’ll just catch sight of myself before I’m leaving, and then I get stuck there.

Like if I’ve got a loan meeting, or I’m going to sit at a craft-fair table where people are going to be walking by and looking at things up close, I’ll check the bathroom mirror before I go out. Then I’ll get out to the truck and check the mirror there too. I’ll turn my hat one way, then the other, pull it down a little, push it back up, trying to see if it makes my face look less weathered or less saggy. And then I’ll look at my hands on the steering wheel and start thinking they look cracked and spotted and old.

Sometimes if younger guys are around the farm, I’ll catch myself comparing my hands to theirs. Not in a normal passing way, either. I mean I’ll actually be looking at how smooth theirs look, or how they don’t have the same kind of marks, and then I feel worse. And meanwhile I’m wasting time I should be using on chores or getting ready to leave. I’ll be standing there checking and rechecking like somehow I’m going to find an angle where it doesn’t look so bad.

So yes, even when nobody’s pointed it out, I still focus on it. I probably point it out to myself enough for everyone.
Have you ever tried to hide or cover up the way your hands or face look, or done things like wearing certain clothes or using makeup to make them less noticeable?

Yes, I do, though I don’t really use makeup or anything like that. It’s more… little things I do trying to make it less obvious. Before I leave for a loan meeting, or if I’m going to be at a craft-fair table where people are going to be close enough to see my hands, I’ll get caught up checking myself.

I’ll look in the bathroom mirror, then I’ll get out to the truck and check that mirror too. I’ll turn my hat one way, then another, pull it down lower, push it back a bit, trying to see if it hides my face better or makes me look less weathered. Sometimes I’ll spend way too long doing that, like it’s going to suddenly fix how I look from one angle.

And with my hands, it’s harder to cover them because I have to use them. So I end up looking at them on the steering wheel or while I’m getting things ready, and then I’ll compare them to the younger workers’ hands if they’re around. Their hands look smoother, cleaner, not so worn out, and then I start thinking mine look even worse. I know that’s not exactly “covering up,” but it’s all part of the same thing for me — trying to figure out how noticeable it is and whether there’s some way to make it not be the first thing people see.

I’ve wasted time doing it, too. Time I should’ve been using on the farm or getting ready to leave, and instead I’m standing there messing with my hat and checking mirrors like I’m going to find the right version of myself before I walk out.

When you think about the way your face or hands look, do you find yourself having the same upsetting thoughts over and over, like a loop in your mind, even when you’re alone and not around other people?

Yes… yes, that’s probably the biggest part of it, honestly. It’s not only when I’m sitting across from someone. It starts before that, and it keeps going after, and sometimes it’s just there when I’m by myself.

I’ll be alone and still thinking, my face looks too weathered, my hands look too rough, the cracks and spots are obvious, the sagging is obvious. It just kind of circles around in my head. Like I can be doing something ordinary and I’ll suddenly picture how I must look to a banker, or somebody from the county office, or anyone who’s used to dealing with people who look cleaner or more put together. And then I’m right back in it, thinking they must be staring at my hands or my face and deciding I look worn down or careless.

My wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors his whole life, and I know she means that to be reassuring. Part of me can hear that. But it doesn’t settle it for me. I keep coming back to the same thought that they don’t just see a working man — they see the cracks, the spots, the sagging, the roughness. And once that thought gets going, it’s hard for me to get past it. It feels like it sticks, even if there’s nobody in the room looking at me at all.

Would you say your main concern is about specific defects or flaws in your appearance that you believe are noticeable to others, or is it more about feeling uncomfortable or anxious in social situations regardless of how you look?

It’s more the first one, I think. I mean, I do get uncomfortable around people, but it doesn’t feel like it starts as just being nervous socially for no reason. It’s tied right to how I think I look.

What brings me in is that I can’t seem to get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. The cracks in my hands, the spots, the sagging in my face — those are the things I keep thinking people notice. Like if I’m sitting with a banker or talking to someone from the county office, I’m not just thinking, “Oh, this is awkward.” I’m thinking, “They’re looking at my hands,” or “They can see how weathered my face is,” or “I look older and more worn down than I should.”

My wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors his whole life, and I know she means that kindly. And part of me understands that’s probably how she sees it. But it doesn’t land that way in my own head. To me it feels like those specific things stand out, like they’re what people see first, even if nobody says anything. So yes, it’s really about those flaws, or what I see as flaws, more than just being anxious around people in general.

doctor.question: When you think about the way your face or hands look, do you find yourself having the same upsetting thoughts over and over, like a loop in your mind, even when you’re alone and not around other people?

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, that’s probably the biggest part of it, honestly. It’s not only when I’m sitting across from someone. It starts before that, and it keeps going after, and sometimes it’s just there when I’m by myself.

I’ll be alone and still thinking, my face looks too weathered, my hands look too rough, the cracks and spots are obvious, the sagging is obvious. It just kind of circles around in my head. Like I can be doing something ordinary and I’ll suddenly picture how I must look to a banker, or somebody from the county office, or anyone who’s used to dealing with people who look cleaner or more put together. And then I’m right back in it, thinking they must be staring at my hands or my face and deciding I look worn down or careless.

My wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors his whole life, and I know she means that to be reassuring. Part of me can hear that. But it doesn’t settle it for me. I keep coming back to the same thought that they don’t just see a working man — they see the cracks, the spots, the sagging, the roughness. And once that thought gets going, it’s hard for me to get past it. It feels like it sticks, even if there’s nobody in the room looking at me at all.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's concerns about his appearance meet the criteria for a preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance, which would support a diagnosis of body dysmorphic disorder (F45.22), as opposed to social anxiety disorder (F40.11), where the primary concern is about being negatively evaluated in social situations more broadly.
doctor.question: Would you say your main concern is about specific defects or flaws in your appearance that you believe are noticeable to others, or is it more about feeling uncomfortable or anxious in social situations regardless of how you look?

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance

patient.answer:
It’s more the first one, I think. I mean, I do get uncomfortable around people, but it doesn’t feel like it starts as just being nervous socially for no reason. It’s tied right to how I think I look.

What brings me in is that I can’t seem to get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. The cracks in my hands, the spots, the sagging in my face — those are the things I keep thinking people notice. Like if I’m sitting with a banker or talking to someone from the county office, I’m not just thinking, “Oh, this is awkward.” I’m thinking, “They’re looking at my hands,” or “They can see how weathered my face is,” or “I look older and more worn down than I should.”

My wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors his whole life, and I know she means that kindly. And part of me understands that’s probably how she sees it. But it doesn’t land that way in my own head. To me it feels like those specific things stand out, like they’re what people see first, even if nobody says anything. So yes, it’s really about those flaws, or what I see as flaws, more than just being anxious around people in general.
